transcript:
Meeting header
2025-09-15 16:00 UTC — Duration: 58m
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Ibrahim Noor (Redwood CSM); Amir Patel (CISO, Helix), Lena Torres (Head Cloud Ops), Priya Singh (SRE), Devon McKay (Legal)

Summary section (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Redwood walked Helix through incident response and business continuity. Discussed RTO/RPO targets, how Redwood Dedicated and Private handle failover, what audit logs look like, SSO and RBAC scopes, and escalation contacts including PD integration. Next steps and action items at end.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: ok, thanks everyone for joining. I think we wanted to keep this focused on B C D R and the SLA/escalation flow, Amir, is that still the core ask?
[00:10] Amir: yeah, thanks Jordan. We're doing a vendor security deep-dive and we need to confirm what RTO and RPO we can expect, how quickly Redwood can failover between regions, and what the on-call path looks like. Also need SOC2/ISO evidence for procurement.
[00:25] Jordan: absolutely. Maya will talk through the runtime behaviors and the escalation hooks. Ibrahim will handle the compliance artifacts.
[00:33] Maya: hi all. Quick note, some transcriptions of product names tend to get messy, so when I say K V cache that's K-V cache, and Redwood Private is our VPC/on-prem option.
[00:43] Priya: cool. we have a strict RTO target for core inference calls of 15 minutes for failover and RPO of 5 minutes for queue metadata. Is that realistic?
[00:55] Maya: so that breaks down a bit. For Hosted API we depend on multi-region routing, and typical cross-region failover for stateless requests is often sub-5 minutes for connectivity, but session state and KV cache warmup is slower. For Dedicated or Private you can get faster predictable failover because you control or reserve capacity. 15 minutes RTO for degraded but functional failover is reasonable if you accept some token-latency spikes while caches warm.
[01:30] Lena: when you say caches warm, is that client-visible? like will requests suddenly take 2-3 seconds per token? Our SLA for customer-facing features is tight — any spike over 500ms is problematic.
[01:42] Maya: yes, there will be transient latency spikes; we use prefix caching and warmup hints to reduce that. For very low latency SLAs we recommend a small hot-standby in region or reserved Dedicated capacity.
[01:55] Amir: also we need to know RPO — you said 5 mins for queue metadata, but what about embeddings and persisted logs?
[02:05] Maya: embeddings stored in customer-managed datastore aren't impacted. For platform-side ephemeral caches the RPO is near zero since it's not durable; for durable ingestion pipelines we recommend log shipping to customer S3 or ELK with retention policies.
[02:22] Jordan: to be explicit: for mission critical, best practice is to use Dedicated with cross-region replication of user data plus customer-side backups. That meets Helix's tighter RPO needs.
[02:35] Devon: legal question — what does your SLA credit model look like? is it the typical service credit ladder or flat refunds? also maintenance windows?
[02:45] Jordan: our standard SLA is 99.9% monthly for Hosted, 99.95% for Dedicated, and enterprise tiers can go higher with ETAs. Credits are tiered: 99.9% down to 99.0% map to X% credits, etc. Maintenance windows are scheduled, we give 72h notice for planned major upgrades; emergency maintenance is rare and communicated via email and status.redwood.ai.
[03:10] Amir: can we get a redlined summary from legal?
[03:15] Jordan: yes Jordan: we'll provide a distilled SLA summary for legal review — action item noted.
[03:20] Maya: on escalation: our PD (PagerDuty) integration can create incidents at severity levels one through four. We recommend severity 1 for complete service outage affecting production. The on-call chain goes Redwood infra -> infra lead -> SE oncall -> AE escalation and finally exec 2nd-level pager. We'll share a diagram.
[03:45] Priya: do you publish runbooks for escalations?
[03:48] Maya: yes, we keep internal runbooks and we can share a redacted playbook excerpt that shows steps: initial detection, auto-recovery attempts, fail to standby, manual failover steps, and communication templates. The full runbook has sensitive internals so we only share a summary.
[04:05] Lena: about audit logs: retention and access controls are critical. We need immutable logs for six months, and ability to pull for audits within 24h. How do you handle that?
[04:16] Ibrahim: we store audit trails in an append-only system with tamper evidence. For Hosted customers we can configure retention and export; for Dedicated/Private customers you can integrate with your SIEM. We'll send sample log records.
[04:30] Amir: does Redwood support customer-managed keys? we need HSM-backed KMS and key rotation policies under our control.
[04:36] Maya: yes, for Private deployments you can use your KMS/HSM through our integrations. For Hosted we offer customer-managed keys via major KMS providers; keys are never stored in cleartext and access is logged. There are some nuances with cross-region key replication which we'll detail.
[04:55] Devon: is there forensic support post-incident? i.e. we want root cause analysis reports and indemnity clauses.
[05:02] Jordan: we provide incident summaries and RCA for Sev1s; indemnity is in contract negotiation. We'll share sample RCAs (redacted).
[05:12] Amir: what about data residency? Helix requires EU-only processing for EU patients. How do you guarantee that?
[05:20] Maya: we can pin tenancy to region and disable cross-region routing for those tenants; telemetry and backups can be configured to remain in-region. For Hosted customers we have EU regions and we can set policies to keep data in EU.
[05:34] Priya: if a region goes down, will you failover outside EU or will you quarantine?
[05:40] Maya: by default we failover to nearest healthy region; but for regulated workloads we can opt for a strict regional-only strategy which will degrade availability but preserve residency. That decision has to be part of the config.
[05:55] Lena: ok, we need to decide tradeoffs — uptime vs residency.
[06:00] Amir: moving on to incident notification cadence: what's your SLA for initial ack and full resolution updates?
[06:08] Maya: initial ack for Sev1 incidents is within 15 minutes, updates every 30 minutes until mitigated, with a post-incident RCA within 5 business days.
[06:18] Jordan: note these are contractual at enterprise tier; we can include tighter comms in a managed SLA.
[06:24] Devon: can you tie alerts to our Jira or PagerDuty as well as email?
[06:28] Maya: yes, integrations are standard — we do PagerDuty, Slack, Jira, ServiceNow.
[06:34] Amir: curious about monitoring signals you use to detect incidents; do you have blackbox tests that exercise the full path?
[06:40] Maya: we use synthetic traffic, end-to-end health checks, latency percentiles, request error rates, and KV cache hit rates. Customers can provide their own probes as well.
[06:48] Lena: for B C D R verification, can we run a tabletop and then a failover drill? we want evidence of RTO meeting during a simulated outage.
[06:56] Jordan: absolutely. We propose a two-step: tabletop to agree playbook, then a runbook-driven failover drill in a staging environment. We'll time the RTO and capture artifacts.
[07:08] Priya: will we be allowed to trigger any forced failovers in production?
[07:12] Maya: forced production failovers are possible but gated — need approvals from both sides, and we suggest doing it in a dedicated maintenance window with monitoring and rollback steps.
[07:22] Amir: about evidence, what artifacts do you produce after drills?
[07:26] Maya: timeline logs, pager notes, synthetic traffic traces, and a measured RTO/RPO table. Also any identified gaps with mitigations.
[07:35] Devon: legal will want that in writing for the pilot agreement.
[07:38] Jordan: noted.
[07:41] Amir: one more on encryption: how long do audit logs last, can we request immutability windows, and how are key rotations handled without causing service disruption?
[07:52] Ibrahim: we support configurable retention; immutability windows can be set by policy for Hosted customers. For key rotation we do staged rotations with dual-key acceptance to avoid downtime; SE will share the rotation diagram.
[08:06] Maya: small caveat, for some older model kernels there is a short window where in-flight cache entries need to be re-encrypted; we handle that automatically, but we capture metrics during rotation.
[08:18] Priya: ok that's fine as long as we get notice.
[08:21] Amir: on escalation, who do we call after hours?
[08:24] Maya: PagerDuty primary. We maintain a 24/7 oncall. For high-severity incidents we escalate to the infra lead and then account exec.
[08:33] Lena: for our compliance team we need a clear phone tree or email alias, a 24/7 security contact.
[08:38] Jordan: we'll include a sample phone tree and the alias.
[08:42] Devon: about indemnity, we'll send proposed language; we need a representation that you keep customer data separation and you have SOC2 controls over access.
[08:50] Ibrahim: yes SOC2 covers logical access controls; we'll send the attestation and mapping to your control set.
[08:58] Amir: is there a support SLA for security incidents separate from availability SLA?
[09:03] Jordan: yes, we can define a security incident response SLA with different comms cadence and escalation.
[09:09] Priya: do you provide chain-of-custody for forensics?
[09:12] Maya: we can produce logs and hashes for evidence, and work with third-party forensics if needed.
[09:18] Amir: ok great. can we talk briefly about multitenancy isolation? Helm chart or namespacing? we need assurance at container and network level.
[09:28] Maya: Dedicated gives tenant isolation via dedicated GPU pools and network level segmentation; Private gives you full control. For Hosted we use tenant namespace isolation and strong RBAC. We'll send architecture notes.
[09:40] Lena: how do you handle role management and least privilege? SSO with SAML or OIDC?
[09:45] Maya: we support SAML SSO, OIDC, SCIM provisioning for users and groups, and RBAC policies that map to roles. Audit logs record admin actions.
[09:54] Devon: any compliance artifacts for SCIM and SSO?
[09:57] Ibrahim: we'll include integration guides and test scripts.
[10:02] Jordan: quick pause — I want to make sure we captured the ask: 1) share SOC2/ISO certs, 2) redacted runbook excerpt, 3) failover diagram & PD integration guide, 4) schedule tabletop and drill, 5) SLA summary for legal.
[10:17] Amir: yes that's right. Also show KMS/HSM key lifecycle and how we can hold keys.
[10:23] Maya: noted.
[10:25] Jordan: any final questions?
[10:28] Priya: what's the rough timeline to run the tabletop and then a failover drill?
[10:32] Jordan: tabletop within 2-3 weeks, failover drill in a staging environment 2-3 weeks after tabletop; total ~6 weeks to complete both if schedules align.
[10:43] Lena: that works. We'll aim for week of 10/6 for tabletop.
[10:47] Amir: please include our security contact in invites — Devon will coordinate legal review.
[10:52] Jordan: will do. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts.

- Maya to attach failover/DR diagram, PagerDuty integration steps, and key rotation diagram by 2025-09-19
- Schedule tabletop for week of 2025-10-06 — Ibrahim to send calendar invite
